title: First word: shalom

segments.voice: Yesterday, nikud: the dots and lines that tell the voice how to read. Your line was the dots. What did you notice yourself filling in? Today, the letters and the dots come together into a whole word. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-three.

Four letters. For weeks now they've been arriving one at a time. Shin, the letter on the door. Lamed, the tall one that rises above the line. Vav, the hook, a single upright stroke. And mem, water, in the closed square shape it takes at the end of a word, one of the five endings. Each one met on its own day, like strangers at a long table. Today they sit down together, side by side, right to left, with two small marks to give them a voice. And they make a word said at doors, written in letters, and found at the end of the priestly blessing. Your first Hebrew word, read on your own.
screen: `FOUR LETTERS, MET ONE BY ONE.` → `RIGHT TO LEFT.` → `TWO SMALL MARKS.` → `YOUR FIRST WORD.`

segments.voice: Shalom. Read it four ways. First, from the right. Hebrew runs right to left, so start at the right edge. Shin, with its three arms. Look at the dot on top: on the right arm, it says sh. On the left arm, it would say s. Here it's on the right. Under it, a small T-shaped mark that, in the pronunciation used in Israel, says ah. Sha. Second, the middle. Lamed, reaching up. Then vav, and right on top of the vav, a single dot. That dot turns the vav into a vowel: oh. Lo. Third, the end. The closed square of final mem, which just says m. Sha, lo, m. Shalom. Fourth, where it lives. In Numbers, at the end of the priestly blessing, the last words are "and give thee peace," and in the Hebrew, the last word is shalom. In the Psalms, the line is "seek peace, and pursue it." And in daily life, it's a hello and a goodbye, and it begins the greeting shalom aleichem, peace be upon you. One word, used at the door coming in and the door going out. In a few days we'll open the root underneath it. For now, the job is simpler: the letters, the dots, and your own voice putting them together.
screen: `SHIN, AND THE DOT ON THE RIGHT.` · `LAMED, THEN VAV WITH A DOT ON TOP.` · `FINAL MEM CLOSES THE WORD.` · `SHALOM AT THE DOOR, IN AND OUT.` · then, large: `שָׁלוֹם`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read the word shalom. Settle, and breathe. Look at the word on the screen. Start at the right. Find the shin and its dot. Find the tall lamed. Find the vav with its dot. Find the closed mem at the end. Now read it slowly, the way a child does the first time: sha, lo, m. Then once more, whole: shalom. Let it sit. If there's someone you'd say it to, bring them to mind as you say it. If you pray, you can hold that word for a moment as you sit. The bell holds the time.
First word. Shalom: shin, lamed, vav, final mem, the first Hebrew word you've read yourself, letter by letter. Today's word.
Your line: shalom, read. Today, say shalom to one person, coming in or going out, and know you can read it. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: Jewish children learning to read Hebrew sound out words letter by letter with the vowel points; shalom is used as a greeting for hello and goodbye, and in the longer greeting shalom aleichem.

what a scholar hears: the priestly blessing in Numbers 6 ends on this word: "and give thee peace."
